title: Standard Gibbs Energies of Formation Can Be Used to Calculate Equilibrium Constants
lead: Tables of standard Gibbs energies of formation give the standard reaction Gibbs energy of any reaction, and through it the equilibrium constant. Ions in water need a reference of their own, since no formation reaction can be written for a single ion.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page, which comes from Howard DeVoe's Thermodynamics and Chemistry.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise and its solution are AI-written, from the standard reaction Gibbs energy the book gives for ammonia in Section 26.6. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.source_id: the tabulated values enable us to evaluate
exercises.prompt:
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), $\kDeltarGstd = -32.9$ kJ/mol at 298.15 K.

  1. What is the standard Gibbs energy of formation of NH₃(g)?
  2. What is the equilibrium constant $K$ of the reaction at 298.15 K?

parts.hint: The elements N₂ and H₂ in their standard states have a Gibbs energy of formation of zero.

answer.solution:
(a) By Equation 26.3.5, $\kDeltarGstd = 2\kDeltafGstd(\text{NH}_3) - \kDeltafGstd(\text{N}_2) - 3\kDeltafGstd(\text{H}_2)$, and the elements contribute zero, so $\kDeltafGstd(\text{NH}_3) = -32.9/2 = -16.45$ kJ/mol.

(b) $K = e^{-\kDeltarGstd/\kR\kT} = \exp\left(\dfrac{32\,900\ \text{J/mol}}{(8.314\ \text{J/(mol K)})(298.15\ \text{K})}\right) = e^{13.27} = 5.81\times10^{5}$.

footnotes.html: This page is Section 11.8 of Howard DeVoe's Thermodynamics and Chemistry, and its references are to that book: Eq. 9.2.46, Sec. 11.3.2, Sec. 6.2, Sec. 14.3.3 and Appendix H are DeVoe's. His Equations 11.8.20 to 11.8.31 are numbered 26.3.1 to 26.3.12 here, so Eq. 11.8.22, 11.8.23 and 11.8.24 are Equations 26.3.3, 26.3.4 and 26.3.5.

derivations.what: the Gibbs energy of formation of a cation
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 26.3 Standard Gibbs Energies of Formation Can Be Used to Calculate Equilibrium Constants

then.why: The reaction is the hypothetical formation of the cation from the elements and aqueous H⁺, each species in its standard state.
